It is interesting to observe that in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries these same gentlemen were busy in promoting a theory of generation which required animalculae within the sperms to be the seat of generation.
The sperm and the egg were looked upon as two halves of an original whole—a ‘prae-embryo’ or animalcule, which was the primordial germ of the individual.
According to such theory, an animalcula is generated in each female, and that only the animalculum from the sperm can fertilize the egg of the female.
This view led to the idea of the primordial germ, or primordia (i.e., germ cells or animalcula).
In 1751, Swammerdam proposed the theory that the spermatozoon was a miniature organism called an animalcula, or animalcule.
According to the theory, this germinal animalcule was contained by the blood and carried about in the veins.
The animalcule is the miniature of man, from which the whole human body was generated.
As to the generation of the human animalcule, the idea that its first appearance in utero was through the agency of the female germ, rather than the male, did not take root at once.
Animalcules (spermatozoa) were described as having an inner gelatinous envelope, and a gelatinous nucleus.
The conception of sperm as animalcules is now regarded with great embarrassment, but the idea of an individual, preformed human germ, has its modern advocates.
According to the former concept, the male sperm and female egg were only two aspects of an individual cell from which there would be no increase in number. Thus, it was not ‘sperm’ but ‘animalcule’.
